questions.q: Name the three main categories of IUDs available in India's National Family Planning Programme and give one example of each with its effective lifespan.
questions.a: The three categories are: (1) Non-medicated/inert IUDs — e.g., Lippes Loop (effective ~3-5 years, now largely phased out); (2) Copper-releasing IUDs — e.g., Cu-T 380A / Cu-7 / Multiload-375 (effective 5-10 years); (3) Hormone-releasing IUDs — e.g., LNG-20 / Mirena (levonorgestrel-releasing, effective 5 years). A wrong answer (e.g., listing "condom" as an IUD type or confusing Cu-T with hormonal IUD) reveals the student cannot distinguish device mechanisms and relies on rote memorization without understanding the classification basis (mode of action: physical barrier vs copper toxicity vs local progestin release).

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with a history of migraine with aura asks for contraception. Why are combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) containing estrogen CONTRAINDICATED for her, while a copper IUD or progestin-only pill would be safer? Explain the physiological mechanism.
questions.a: Estrogen in COCPs increases synthesis of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) and decreases antithrombin III, creating a hypercoagulable state. Migraine with aura is an independent risk factor for ischemic stroke; the combination multiplies thrombotic risk (synergistic, not additive). Copper IUD acts locally via copper ions toxic to sperm/ova — no systemic hormones. Progestin-only pill (mini-pill) lacks estrogen, so no increased clotting risk; it works mainly by thickening cervical mucus and suppressing endometrium. A wrong answer citing "estrogen causes migraine" or "pills cause blood clots in everyone" shows confusion between side effect and absolute contraindication, and ignorance of the specific pathophysiological link (estrogen → hepatic coagulation cascade modulation).

questions.q: A couple wants a reversible method with >99% effectiveness that does not require daily adherence. They have completed their family but may want a child in 3 years. Which single method best fits, and why would a hormonal IUD (LNG-20) be preferable to a copper IUD for a woman who also has heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia)?
questions.a: Hormonal IUD (LNG-20/Mirena) is the best fit: >99% effective (Pearl Index ~0.1-0.2), reversible (fertility returns within 1-3 months after removal), lasts 5 years (covers their 3-year window), no daily action needed. For menorrhagia: LNG-20 releases levonorgestrel locally → endometrial atrophy → reduces menstrual blood loss by 80-90% (therapeutic benefit). Copper IUD often increases menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhea (copper-induced prostaglandin release → uterine contractions). A wrong answer suggesting "vasectomy" (not easily reversible), "COCP" (requires daily adherence, lower typical-use effectiveness ~91%), or "copper IUD for menorrhagia" (worsens it) shows inability to match method attributes to patient-specific clinical scenarios.

questions.q: Compare the mechanism of action of Centchroman (Ormeloxifene, "Saheli") with that of a combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP). Why is Centchroman taken twice a week for 3 months then once a week, whereas COCP is taken daily for 21 days followed by 7 pill-free days?
questions.a: Centchroman is a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM): it antagonizes estrogen receptors in uterus (prevents endometrial proliferation → implantation failure) and breast, but agonizes in bone (prevents osteoporosis). It does NOT suppress ovulation consistently; primary action is anti-implantation. Its long half-life (~160 hours) allows weekly dosing after loading phase. COCP contains ethinyl estradiol + progestin: suppresses ovulation via negative feedback on HPO axis (daily dosing needed to maintain steady hormone levels for 21 days); 7-day break induces withdrawal bleed. A wrong answer stating "Centchroman is a progestin" or "both prevent ovulation" reveals confusion between SERM pharmacology and steroid hormone contraception, and ignorance of dosing rationale tied to pharmacokinetics.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs) containing levonorgestrel 1.5 mg are a form of regular contraception and can be used multiple times per cycle." Identify the biological and programmatic errors.
questions.a: The statement is FALSE on two counts: (1) Biological: ECPs are high-dose progestin (levonorgestrel 1.5 mg or ulipristal acetate 30 mg) taken within 72-120h post-coitus; they primarily delay/prevent ovulation if taken pre-ovulation. Repeated use in one cycle causes hormonal disruption — irregular bleeding, unpredictable ovulation — and lower efficacy than regular methods. (2) Programmatic: ECPs are for EMERGENCY use only (condom break, sexual assault, missed pills); they have higher failure rate (~10-25%) vs regular COCP (~0.3% perfect use). WHO and India's guidelines restrict ECP to occasional use. A student agreeing with the statement confuses "contraception" (planned, ongoing prevention) with "emergency backup" and ignores the endocrine disruption from frequent high-dose progestin exposure.

questions.q: Design a counseling flowchart for a 35-year-old woman (smoker, BMI 32, controlled hypertension on medication) seeking contraception. At each decision node, state the clinical criterion and the method recommended/rejected with biological justification.
questions.a:
Flowchart logic: 
Start → Age >35 + Smoker? YES → Estrogen-containing methods (COCP, patch, ring) REJECTED (synergistic thrombotic risk: estrogen ↑ clotting factors + smoking → endothelial damage + age → ↑ baseline CVD risk). 
→ Hypertension (controlled)? YES → Further avoids estrogen (estrogen ↑ angiotensinogen → ↑ BP). 
→ BMI >30? YES → COCP efficacy reduced (hepatic metabolism ↑, volume of distribution ↑); also VTE risk ↑ with obesity. 
→ Recommended: Progestin-only methods (POP, DMPA injection, hormonal IUD LNG-20, implant) — no estrogen, safe in all above conditions. Copper IUD also safe (non-hormonal). 
→ Surgical (tubectomy) if family complete. 
A poor flowchart that recommends COCP "because she's on BP meds" or rejects IUD "due to obesity" shows failure to apply WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) categories and misunderstanding of estrogen-specific vs progestin-specific risks.
